subject: Proposal for new R package - Looking for a mentor

messages.author: 394d0708815c45c7
messages.subject: Proposal for new R package - Looking for a mentor
parts:
R package: DiscovR


Background: The main advantage of R compared to languages as Python or Matlab are its ability to analyze datasets in a fast and intuitive way. Working on different projects in the field of molecular life science, I often felt a shortcoming in R packages in the data exploration part.

Taking the analysis pipeline: Data Import – first Exploration – Analysis – Statistical/Graphical output

The exploration often only includes the checking for NAs, wrong datatypes (such as chars) and the general structure of the dataset. The process is then continued by checking for correlations / glm / lm / nls / random forests / PCA, and more.


My point here is that we could greatly enhance the R working experience in the first exploration step by creating a new package, which allows for a fast inspection of the viability to use the most common statistical techniques and packages. The “viability” of analysis techniques can be either determined by p-values / AIC-values / or in cases of Bayes statistics by the relative branching number.

The general idea is thereby to show what can actually be done with your data – and then decide what for your purpose is useful to continue to do.


To the package design itself:


The syntax of the package should follow the style of common packages:


discovr(x, data = dataframe, options = c(xyz))


Whereby the x argument represents the dependent rows, while all other columns of the dataframe are used as independent rows. If no argument x is given, general aspects are analyzed, such as the effect of transformations of the rows on the correlation coefficients etc..

The Output is either a D3 interactive heat map, with a color range green to red indicating the viability of the techniques, or an integer output, similar to lm() with discovr.variable$results as example.


Challenges & rewards: As the viability of analysis techniques for datasets is often difficult to predict in terms of integer values alone, smart consumptions have to been taken, which may be a combination of different statistical methods itself. As those challenges are solved, It will allow R users an enhanced experience when analyzing datasets: Knowing beforehand, if techniques, which conditions are rarely met, may actually be applicable for the dataset you analyze.   


My experience: As a biochemistry graduate student, I worked for two departments, seeing the effectiveness of R in practical work and used those data to publish biomedical articles. Thereby, I wrote a shiny application (~1000 lines of code), which streamlined microscopic time series analysis. I took most Datacamp.com courses and am daily looking for r-bloggers new articles to improve my coding skills. 


Mentors: As first mentor im looking for someone experienced in the general R package design and general good skills in R programming.


As second mentor I would suggest a post doc from my university, who knows the actual needs for the scientific work with datasets. His part would be to make sure that the package is viable to be used and accurate in its underlying statistics.

Many thanks for sharing your ideas for a proposal.

My point here is that we could greatly enhance the R working experience in the first exploration step by creating a new package, which allows for a fast inspection of the viability to use the most common statistical techniques and packages. The “viability” of analysis techniques can be either determined by p-values / AIC-values / or in cases of Bayes statistics by the relative branching number.

I usually have a more focused approach to exploratory data analysis, where instead of running a whole set of methods I pick the ones I find most appropriate. In any case, I believe that there might be some other packages for exploratory data analysis that you should take into account so that your proposal is about implementing something new. I am not able to provide any but perhaps other people on this list can.

As second mentor I would suggest a post doc from my university, who knows the actual needs for the scientific work with datasets. His part would be to make sure that the package is viable to be used and accurate in its underlying statistics.

That could be fine, but he will need to register and get involved in the whole GSoC thing. Once we have all the proposals on-line we ask mentors to comment on them and vote.

Best wishes,

Virgilio
